2026.problem: Graph-based recommendation systems ignore negative user signals like dislikes, missing critical preference information.
2026.approach: SPGNN extends GNNs with signed local/global proximity metrics rooted in weak balance theory to capture sign-aware multi-scale node relations.
2026.contribution: Significantly improves top-K recommendation accuracy in signed graphs by unlocking sign-aware neighborhood aggregation and feature initialization.
2026.bp: Real users like and dislike items—recommendations ignore dislikes at their peril. Today most systems only learn from positive signals, missing half the story. SPGNN realizes that dislikes are data too.
2026.wh: Standard GNNs aggregate all neighbor signals equally, treating dislikes as noise. Transformer approaches see the full graph but waste computation and struggle with sign patterns. Neither path captures the local geometry of positive and negative ties.
2026.ap: SPGNN brings two ideas: first, it measures proximity locally (among nearby nodes) and globally (through long paths) while respecting plus and minus signs. Second, it initializes node features thoughtfully, grounded in balance theory—a principle saying users avoid contradiction (liking A who dislikes B).
2026.ww: Proximity that respects sign structure naturally reflects how real preferences propagate. A user who dislikes a category will skew away from items that category approves of. By encoding this locally and globally, the model learns richer representations faster.
2026.po: Experiments show SPGNN beats prior signed-graph work on recommendation tasks. It lifts top-K accuracy by modeling the structural role of negative feedback—what dislikes really mean in the context of a user's web of preferences.

2027.problem: LLMs simulate human behavior poorly because pretraining on static web data lacks situated individual context spanning time.
2027.approach: HumanLLM builds a Cognitive Genome Dataset from 5.5M user logs on Reddit/Twitter/Amazon, fine-tunes an LLM to predict personalized thoughts and behaviors.
2027.contribution: Foundation model for individual-level human simulation and personalization, enabling social science insights and customer behavior prediction.
2027.bp: Understanding one person's decision-making—not average behavior, but *this person's* next move—opens doors to better social science and customer insights. LLMs are trained on the aggregate; what if we taught them to think like individuals?
2027.wh: Standard LLMs see billions of words but no continuity of a single life. They learn statistical patterns across humanity but lose the narrative arc—yesterday's decision shapes today's mood shapes tomorrow's choice. That continuity is invisible in web text.
2027.ap: HumanLLM curates real user timelines from platforms: Reddit posts, tweets, reviews, comments over weeks or months. It cleans and synthesizes these into profiles of beliefs, preferences, and reasoning patterns. Then it fine-tunes a base LLM on tasks like 'given this person's history, what will they do next?'
2027.ww: A person's past is the best predictor of their future. By seeing coherent trajectories (not just snapshots), the model learns that context matters. When you know someone thinks X about politics, Y about food, and has a pattern of Z reasoning, you can extrapolate accurately.
2027.po: Benchmarks show HumanLLM predicts individual behaviors far better than baseline LLMs. The payoff: social researchers can simulate synthetic populations; companies can tailor experiences to *you*, not to the median user.

2028.problem: Offline RL for auto-bidding learns from suboptimal historical data, limiting policy improvement despite expensive hyperparameter tuning.
2028.approach: QGA combines Q-value regularized Decision Transformer with dual-exploration mechanism, using Q-guidance to balance imitation and optimization.
2028.contribution: Improves bidding policies by joint optimization of experience imitation and action-value maximization, with principled exploration beyond data distribution.
2028.bp: E-commerce lives on ad auctions: every millisecond, a bid decision. Bidding too high wastes money; too low loses sales. Advertisers want automation that learns from their past bids yet finds better strategies than what history shows.
2028.wh: Past bids reflect budget limits, mistakes, and outdated beliefs—not wisdom. An RL agent trained purely to mimic history gets stuck in local optima. But ignoring history entirely risks catastrophe (overspending). The tension: trust but transcend.
2028.ap: QGA learns a Q-value function (how good each bid is) alongside a Decision Transformer (how likely each bid was historically). It trains both jointly: the Q-value pulls toward better actions; the transformer ensures those actions stay plausible. To explore safely, it conditions on different 'return targets' and perturbations, always checking each candidate against Q-values before trying it.
2028.ww: Q-values ground speculation. An unexplored bid might help, but only if the model thinks it could pay off. By fusing imitation (we tried this before) with valuation (here's why it's good), the agent escapes local optima without wild swings.
2028.po: On both public benchmarks and real auction simulations, QGA bids more efficiently than imitation-only or vanilla RL. The result: better ROI for advertisers, fewer wasted impressions.

2029.problem: Graph anomaly detection fails on dynamic networks and rare anomalies due to transductive-only models and extreme class imbalance.
2029.approach: Framework with discrete ego-graph diffusion model for anomaly generation and curriculum augmentation to balance data during training.
2029.contribution: Inductive anomaly detection on evolving graphs via anomaly-aware data synthesis and progressive underrepresented sample focusing.
2029.bp: Fraud and cyberattacks hide in network patterns: unusual connections, atypical timing. Real networks evolve—new users, new links—but trained fraud detectors often fail on tomorrow's data. And anomalies are *rare*, so a model trained naively learns to say 'normal' always.
2029.wh: Transductive models assume a static graph; real networks shift daily. Imbalanced training (99.9% normal, 0.1% fraud) teaches models to ignore the rare class. Augmenting the rare class artificially is tempting but risky: fake anomalies might not match real structure.
2029.ap: The framework uses diffusion (the same process that generates images from noise) to learn the local topology of real anomalies. Given a real anomaly, it generates synthetic ego-graphs—neighborhoods around nodes—that preserve structural patterns. During training, it uses a curriculum: early on, focus on abundant anomaly types; later, shift weight toward rare, hard-to-spot variants.
2029.ww: Diffusion captures distributional structure, not just a few examples. A curriculum teaches the model progressively harder cases, like practicing scales before concertos. Together, they produce balanced training data that generalizes to unseen network shifts.
2029.po: On five datasets, the framework detects anomalies better than prior work, especially on new graph structures and rare anomaly patterns. The payoff: fraud systems that adapt as networks evolve.

2030.problem: Multimodal recommendation fuses text, images, video naively, amplifying modality-specific noise and missing distribution shifts between modalities.
2030.approach: DAMPS uses Fast Fourier Transform to decompose multimodal representations into amplitude and phase, then denoises and calibrates both spectra.
2030.contribution: Cleaner fused multimodal representations via spectral domain analysis, improving recommendation accuracy by suppressing modality noise.
2030.bp: A product has a photo (visual), description (text), video (temporal). Blending all three should give richer recommendations. But images carry camera noise, text has language quirks, video has frame artifacts. Today's fusion systems treat all signals equally, amplifying trash.
2030.wh: Each modality lives in its own statistical space. Text embeddings might cluster at scale 0.9, images at 1.2. When you average them, noise from the lower-variance modality screams louder. Also, phases (orientations) can mismatch—two embeddings pointing in opposite directions still average, canceling each other.
2030.ap: DAMPS applies Fourier analysis: decompose each modality's embeddings into amplitude (strength) and phase (direction). For phase, compute the optimal offset between modalities and rotate them into alignment. For amplitude, apply a filter that suppresses low-signal modalities and preserves strong, modality-specific components.
2030.ww: Fourier decomposition separates 'how much' (amplitude) from 'which direction' (phase). Misaligned phases cause destructive interference; fixing them ensures signals add constructively. Amplitude filtering is like tuning a radio: boost clear stations, quiet noisy ones.
2030.po: Benchmarks show DAMPS recommendations improve accuracy over naive fusion. The payoff: recommendation systems that extract signal from multimodal clutter without manual tuning per modality.

2031.problem: Adding edges to reduce total biharmonic distance (network robustness metric) is computationally hard; greedy methods scale cubically.
2031.approach: Greedy algorithms with projection methods, Laplacian solvers, and convex hull approximation to reduce cubic complexity to nearly linear.
2031.contribution: Nearly linear-time link recommendation maintaining error guarantees while preserving network connectivity efficiency at scale.
2031.bp: A network's robustness is how well it stays connected if parts fail. Biharmonic distance measures this: sum all pairwise distances and you get a global connectivity score. Improving it by adding k edges matters for infrastructure, supply chains, and resilience.
2031.wh: Computing which k edges help most requires evaluating every subset. That's exponential. Greedy approximation is tractable but still O(n³)—infeasible for networks with millions of nodes. Theoretical results don't guarantee a good solution, just a bounded error.
2031.ap: The paper proposes greedy algorithms with three acceleration techniques. First, projection: prune edge candidates early. Second, Laplacian solver: use matrix algebra tricks to compute distance changes faster. Third, convex hull: find which edges matter most geometrically, not exhaustively.
2031.ww: Projection eliminates obviously bad candidates early. Laplacian solvers exploit the structure of the distance metric—it's tied to the graph's Laplacian matrix, which has fast algorithms. Convex hulls restrict the search space to candidates on the boundary of feasibility.
2031.po: Scaling from cubic to nearly linear enables biharmonic optimization on real graphs: thousands of nodes, millions of edges. Infrastructure planners can now compute which connections to add for maximum resilience.

2032.problem: Federated learning on heterogeneous data fails: knowledge distillation ensures consistency but limits exploration; models get stuck in bad local optima.
2032.approach: FedKDMR combines dynamic knowledge distillation with model recombination to enable both consistency and diverse parameter exploration.
2032.contribution: Superior accuracy-robustness trade-off in federated learning via joint KD and model perturbation, with convergence guarantees.
2032.bp: Training across hospitals, phones, or edge devices keeps data private. But each site's data differs—patient demographics vary, user behavior differs. A model trained on everyone's data should work everywhere, but heterogeneity breaks optimization.
2032.wh: Knowledge distillation (forcing all local models to match a global teacher) ensures consistency but bakes in the teacher's biases. Local models can't explore far from it, even if better solutions exist. Without distillation, models diverge and forget shared knowledge.
2032.ap: FedKDMR uses dynamic KD: the global model teaches local models, but the strength of that teaching varies. Alongside distillation, it encourages model recombination—systematically perturbing merged parameters to explore the solution space. Local models stay somewhat aligned yet probe new regions.
2032.ww: Perturbation forces exploration; KD prevents divergence. Together, they escape sharp minima. Strong convexity ensures convergence despite perturbations; the averaged updates still march toward a good solution, just more robustly.
2032.po: Benchmarks on federated datasets show FedKDMR beats baseline KD and model averaging. Models converge faster and perform better on held-out heterogeneous data, crucial for privacy-critical deployments.

2033.problem: OOD detection with vision-language models relies on heuristic negative label mining, causing false negatives and missing true out-of-distribution cases.
2033.approach: Theoretical framework correcting sampling bias in negative label selection via approximating negative distribution using Monte Carlo sampling.
2033.contribution: Debiased negative mining improves OOD detection by correcting false negatives; state-of-the-art results across multiple OOD benchmarks.
2033.bp: A model trained on cats and dogs should reject a photo of a giraffe. Vision-language models (which understand both images and text) can compare a photo to words like 'cat' and 'dog'. If neither match well, it's OOD. But picking good 'negative' labels (things the giraffe isn't) is surprisingly hard.
2033.wh: You can't label all OOD examples—there are infinitely many. So you pick heuristic negatives: random words, semantic opposites. But heuristics bias toward easy negatives, missing harder ones. A 'horse' is closer to 'dog' than 'cloud' is. The sampling of negatives is skewed, making OOD detection unreliable.
2033.ap: The paper develops a theory: assume negatives follow an unknown distribution. Correct for sampling bias indirectly by relating the biased sample to the true distribution. Then, convert this into Monte Carlo sampling—simple, efficient. Use labeled in-distribution data and unlabeled wild data to estimate which words are true negatives.
2033.ww: Correcting bias algebraically ensures the negative set reflects the true OOD space, not just the heuristic's blind spots. Monte Carlo provides a practical algorithm: resample from a corrected distribution, not a heuristic list.
2033.po: Experiments across OOD benchmarks show the debiased approach catches more true out-of-distribution cases, raising detection rates while lowering false alarms. The payoff: VLM-based OOD detection suitable for production deployments.

2034.problem: LLM-based function calling for agents incurs redundant processing of function libraries, full-sequence generation, and boilerplate syntax for every call.
2034.approach: HyFunc uses hybrid-model cascade (large model to soft token → retriever → small prefix-tuned model) plus dynamic templating for on-the-fly syntax.
2034.contribution: Inference latency cut by eliminating redundant computation while maintaining accuracy on unseen function-calling benchmarks.
2034.bp: Agentic AI talks to tools: 'call function X with params Y.' Today's pipeline loads a huge LLM, feeds it a fat prompt listing all functions, and waits for it to generate tokens one by one. For real-time apps, this stalls.
2034.wh: The large model processes the entire function library for every query, even though only a few functions are relevant. It generates full token sequences, much of which is repetitive boilerplate (brackets, commas, colons). All three costs are incurred per call.
2034.ap: HyFunc distills a large model into a small 'soft token' (a learned embedding) representing the user's intent. This token goes to a retriever (picking relevant functions) and a smaller prefix-tuned model (generating the final call). Separately, dynamic templating fills in syntactic boilerplate within the vLLM engine, not via token generation.
2034.ww: A soft token captures essence without token overhead. The retriever focuses the context window. A smaller model, given narrowed choices, generates only the semantic content; syntax is injected post-hoc. Each step cuts latency; combined, the speedup is dramatic.
2034.po: On the BFCL benchmark, HyFunc achieves 0.828 second latency with minimal accuracy loss. The payoff: agentic systems that respond instantly to user intents, enabling interactive experiences.

2035.problem: Deep RL for 3D bin packing fails under real-world distribution shifts as batches of goods arrive with different characteristics.
2035.approach: Frames packing as Model Predictive Control solved with MCTS; lookahead parcels inform exploration balance between learned RL and robust random policies.
2035.contribution: 10% gains under distribution shift, 4-8% average online improvement by leveraging available lookahead information via MCTS.
2035.bp: Warehouses pack boxes into trucks using robots. Today, boxes arrive in batches: morning's toys differ from afternoon's electronics. A neural network trained on mixed batches fails when batch characteristics change. Yet lookahead is available—warehouses know tomorrow's shipment types.
2035.wh: Pure DRL learns statistics of all goods but brittle to batch shifts. When morning goods are suddenly heavier or bulkier, the policy collapses. Using lookahead naively (generating fixed plans) ignores the present state. The tension: adapt to now while planning for what's coming.
2035.ap: MCTS, the same algorithm that powers game-playing AI, builds a search tree: 'if I place box A here, then B, then C...' Each node is scored by both the learned RL policy (what's likely good) and a random policy (robust baseline). An auxiliary reward penalizes spatial waste. Lookahead parcels tune the exploration balance—when batches are volatile, trust the random policy more.
2035.ww: MCTS combines foresight (lookahead) with learning (RL policy). The random policy prevents overfitting to training batch statistics. Penalizing waste explicitly prevents short-sighted placements. Adaptive exploration balance lets the algorithm respond to changing conditions.
2035.po: Real-world experiments show 10% gains under distribution shifts and sustained 4-8% improvement in online deployment. The payoff: logistics systems that handle variable conditions robustly, cutting labor and transportation costs.

2036.problem: Session-based recommendation ignores latent neighbors—sessions not directly observed but semantically similar—limiting performance under data sparsity.
2036.approach: DiffSBR generates latent neighbor sessions using retrieval-augmented and self-augmented diffusion modules to synthesize high-quality augmented data.
2036.contribution: Improved session-based recommendation by generating semantically relevant latent neighbors, addressing data sparsity via diffusion-based synthesis.
2036.bp: Online shopping sessions are short: 'user viewed X, Y, Z; what's next?' Two users with similar interests might browse in different orders. Current systems retrieve similar sessions to improve context. But what if the best similar session was never observed?
2036.wh: Real session data is sparse—most session sequences are unique. Neighbors are rare. Retrieving only *observed* neighbors misses the interest space: two sessions might be kindred spirits yet look different superficially (one browsed via search, one via categories).
2036.ap: DiffSBR uses diffusion to imagine latent neighbor sessions. First, a retrieval-augmented module: take observed neighbors as guiding signals, then diffuse (add noise iteratively to a random session, then reverse it) to generate synthetic sessions aligned with real neighbors. Second, self-augmented module: directly diffuse using the current session's signals (text, images) as guidance via contrastive learning.
2036.ww: Diffusion models are known to generate images and text realistically by learning distributions. Here, they learn the distribution of sessions. Conditioning on retrieval guidance ensures variety; conditioning on the current session's multimodal signals ensures relevance. The result: plausible latent neighbors.
2036.po: Experiments show DiffSBR recommends better items than retrieval-only or simple augmentation. The payoff: session-based systems that infer from sparse, noisy histories by synthesizing rich contextual neighbors.

2037.problem: Cross-domain recommendation requires either shared users/items or unrealistic data sharing; existing methods fail under privacy and domain isolation constraints.
2037.approach: MergeRec merges domain-specific models using training-free initialization, pseudo-user data synthesis, and collaborative merging weight optimization.
2037.contribution: Cross-domain sequential recommendation under data isolation via model merging, enabling transfer without sharing raw interactions.
2037.bp: A user browses movies on Netflix, music on Spotify, books on Amazon. Each platform learns preferences separately. Ideally, movie taste informs music taste (sci-fi fans might like synth-pop), yet platforms can't share raw data for privacy.
2037.wh: Prior work assumes overlapping users or items, or needs to share data directly. But privacy regulations forbid sharing user histories. Domain-specific models are isolated; merging them naively loses signal because the models have learned incompatible representations.
2037.ap: MergeRec initializes a merged model using training-free merging (parameter averaging with domain-aware weights). Then, it synthesizes pseudo-user data: treat each item as a virtual user's sequence (if movie A led to movie B in data, a pseudo-user 'liked' A then B). This gives training signal without real users. Finally, optimize merging weights jointly via recommendation loss (merged model ranks correct items) and distillation loss (preserved knowledge from source models).
2037.ww: Pseudo-user data circumvents privacy: you're not synthesizing user identities, just plausible sequences. Training-free initialization starts intelligently. Collaborative weight optimization respects both domains' learned signals while blending them.
2037.po: Experiments show MergeRec transfers knowledge across domains better than baselines, especially in sparse scenarios. The payoff: platforms can improve recommendations via model sharing, not data sharing.

2038.problem: Long-horizon forecasting on large spatial-temporal graphs incurs prohibitive computational costs and memory consumption for deep models.
2038.approach: FaST uses adaptive graph agent attention for efficient convolution and parallel Mixture-of-Experts with GLUs to replace feed-forward networks.
2038.contribution: One-week-ahead predictions on thousand-node graphs via efficient long-horizon spatial-temporal forecasting with strong accuracy-speed trade-offs.
2038.bp: Cities need to forecast traffic or power demand a week ahead across thousands of locations. Spatial-temporal models capture how patterns spread (traffic on Main Street affects Side Street tomorrow). But long horizons multiply computation: each step processes the whole graph.
2038.wh: Standard graph convolution and self-attention scale quadratically or worse with graph size. A week ahead is 672 steps at 15-minute intervals; multiplying by thousands of nodes yields infeasible memory and compute. Models designed for short-term (24-hour) forecasts collapse under this load.
2038.ap: FaST introduces two ideas. First, adaptive graph agent attention: instead of processing all nodes, assign each node an 'agent' that selectively attends to relevant neighbors. This reduces attention cost. Second, parallel Mixture-of-Experts: replace dense feed-forward layers with sparse expert routers and Gated Linear Units (GLUs). Each token routes to a few experts, not all, cutting memory.
2038.ww: Adaptive attention exploits locality: traffic patterns are regional, not global. Sparse routing via MoE works because forecasting doesn't need all parameters per step; different regions use different expertise. GLUs add nonlinearity efficiently.
2038.po: Benchmarks show FaST forecasts accurately week-ahead on real graphs with thousands of nodes, achieving 10× speedup over dense baselines. The payoff: infrastructure operators can forecast long horizons in practice, enabling proactive resource planning.
